Bill Ackman's Pershing Square cut its Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) stake by 35%, according to a 24/7 Wall St. report published November 17. The figure comes from Pershing Square's Form 13F, filed November 16, 2026, and it reflects holdings as of the September 30 quarter-end. A 13F shows quarter-end positions and is released weeks later. It says nothing about trades since then. Pershing Square opened the position in the quarter ended March 31, and the filing gave no reason for the cut.

HJBC / iStock Editorial via Getty Images

A fund manager can adjust a position whenever his view changes. Investors who own Microsoft through index funds follow the index instead. Their funds hold the stock at whatever weight the index sets.

Microsoft Shares Slide Over the Past Week

Microsoft traded at $498.79 as of 10:54 AM ET, down 3.71% in today's regular session. Shares are down 8.51% over the past week and up 3.79% year to date. Today's decline and the Pershing Square filing are separate events. Earlier in the week, the Wall Street Journal reported that Microsoft stock slipped on a widespread outage.

Invesco's QQQM tracks the same Nasdaq-100 index as QQQ for 0.15% versus 0.18%, saving $30 a year on $100,000.

Selling QQQ for QQQM realizes taxable gains, and that bill can dwarf many years of the $30 saving.

Switching inside IRAs and 401(k)s triggers no capital gains tax, making tax-advantaged accounts the clearest place to move into QQQM.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Invesco didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat IVZ. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

If you own the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), you hold a fund whose appeal is easy to see. QQQ puts the Nasdaq's largest non-financial companies into one liquid ticker. QQQ charges an expense ratio of 0.18%, which comes to $180 a year on a $100,000 balance. Invesco (NYSE:IVZ) also runs the Invesco NASDAQ 100 ETF (NASDAQ:QQQM), which tracks the same index for 0.15%, or $150 a year. The $30 annual gap is real but small, so the useful question is who should act on it.

PIKSEL from Getty Images and utah778 from Getty Images
One Index, One Sponsor, Two Price Tags

Both funds' prospectuses name the Nasdaq-100 Index as the underlying index. QQQ's prospectus says the fund tries to track the index's investment results, before fees and expenses. It describes the index as 100 of the largest domestic and international non-financial companies listed on U.S. Nasdaq-affiliated listing exchanges based on market capitalization. QQQ uses full replication, which means it holds every index security at its index weight.

The two funds are tied together on paper. When the index methodology changed on May 1, 2026, Invesco amended both prospectuses in a single supplement dated April 30, 2026.

QQQ is the original. It is large, heavily traded, and the default vehicle for traders and institutions, and Invesco launched QQQM later as a lower-cost version for long-term holders who have no use for QQQ's trading depth.

QQQ sank 3% Monday as NVIDIA tumbled 4% after CEO Jensen Huang resigned, pushing the Nasdaq-100 toward its worst November since 2008.

The worst-since-2008 label vanishes if the index finishes November above about 27,600, roughly 1.5% higher than Monday's close.

Chip stocks carry the fund: the semiconductor index fell 5% Monday with all 30 members lower, and NVIDIA's $3.77 trillion heft sways everything.

The biggest 401k decisions tend to get made once and never revisited: when to roll it over, what to hold inside it, and when to start taking money out. That is exactly what the report: 401k & IRA Tips and Answers was created to address, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

The Nasdaq-100 fell 2.67% on Monday. The index is now down 4.18% for November, with nine trading sessions left.

Wikimedia Commons

Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) also fell 2.67% and closed at $661.75. It rose 0.09% to $662.37 after hours as of 7:59 p.m. ET, and that quote can change before the next open.

AI-focused stocks, which are the market's biggest weights, led the decline. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) fell 4.12% to $156.14. The stock is still absorbing the company's November 12 announcement that Jensen Huang resigned and that CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO.

Policy added to the pressure. Democrats' sweeping midterm wins raised concerns that new AI data center construction could be limited, and the administration issued new rules restricting remote access to advanced U.S. chips and servers.

Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist of Pinpoint Asset Management, said a risk the market was already worried about has become more serious. For QQQ holders, the rest of November carries more weight than usual because the month's historical ranking is still open.

Where This November Ranks Since 1985

Since October 1985, only four Novembers were worse, all during market crises: the 1987 crash (-8.63%), 2000 (-23.63%), 2007 (-6.69%), and 2008 (-11.17%). By contrast, no November from 2009 through 2025 fell more than 2011's -2.75%, and 2025 ended at -1.64%.

Investing.com -- Long global semiconductors remains the most crowded trade among investors, according to Bank of America's November fund manager survey, though the share naming it has fallen sharply from its peak.

Our AI stock portfolio is beating the S&P 500 by 118%. Discover the stocks we're buying and the opportunities we're watching next. Exclusive for Yahoo! Finance readers: 55% off for Black Friday, plus an extra 15% at checkout. Subscribe today! »

Some 39% of respondents named it, well ahead of short China stocks at 14% and long "Magnificent Seven" stocks at 12%. The semiconductor share has declined steadily from a July high of 82%.

Investors cut their tech overweight by the most since 2006, the survey found, as the euphoria around the economic boom and AI is fading, strategists led by Michael Hartnett said.

"We stay tactically risk-off," they wrote, noting that the survey "does not show enough investor 'fear' to buy."

AI spending was a central concern. Some 52% of investors expect an AI hyperscaler to announce a capex cut in the next six months, up from 30% in October. A record net 38% say companies are overinvesting, and just 16% want companies to boost capex, the lowest since May 2020.

Stop chasing stocks after they've already rallied. Find your next investment opportunity with AI stock picks, earnings insights, and market-moving news. Yahoo! Finance readers get an extra 15% off on top of the 55% off Black Friday price. Join today! »

The analysts described the survey's big message as "pause AI capex."

Asked about the biggest tail risk, 34% said an AI bubble and 31% said a hyperscaler credit event. AI hyperscaler bonds were seen as the most likely source of a credit event by 38%, followed by private credit at 30%.

From an economic perspective, 50% of respondents expect a soft landing, overtaking the 42% who see no landing for the first time since June. Only 3% expect a hard landing. Expectations of a "boom" slipped to 41% from 47% in October.

Investors trimmed their bond underweight by 13 percentage points, the biggest monthly increase since April 2025. They remain a net 23% underweight. On average, they said a 10-year Treasury yield of 5.8% would prompt a shift from stocks into bonds.

Average cash levels fell to 3.6% from 3.9%, the lowest since August, while a record net 23% said gold is undervalued.

The survey ran from Nov. 6 to 12 and covered 193 panelists with $526 billion in assets under management.
